Name: Mortise-and-Tenon Assembly of Prefabricated Punic Warships and the Mediterranean Shipbuilding Industry
RagShortTexts: Carthage had the most advanced modular shipbuilding industry in the Mediterranean, with every timber beam carved with a numbered mark
Its shipyards could rapidly assemble dozens of large quinqueremes on a production line within a few dozen days
Rome captured a stranded Punic warship and copied its assembly marks to found shipyards of its own
BaseText: Carthage's ability to maintain its supremacy in the Mediterranean for centuries rested on its highly modern, modular shipbuilding assembly line. On the keel timbers of Punic shipwrecks excavated in Tunisia and at Marsala, archaeologists have found, astonishingly, large numbers of Phoenician letter marks and assembly guide signs carved in advance by craftsmen with chisels. Carthaginian craftsmen prefabricated keels, ribs and hull planks in the inland forests to uniform, standardized specifications, with every timber beam marked with its order of installation and the position of its mortises and tenons. Once these reached the shipsheds of the circular naval harbor, it took only a gathering of skilled carpenters to assemble dozens of excellent quinqueremes on a production line within a few dozen days. Early in the First Punic War, Rome used a stranded and captured Carthaginian warship as its standard model, copied its plank numbering and the geometry of its mortise-and-tenon joints exactly, and within two months miraculously built a great fleet of one hundred ships, breaking the Phoenicians' monopoly on shipbuilding engineering.

Variants.Content: Every cedar beam is carved with secret marks in the ancient letters of Tyre. As long as the slipways of the shipsheds remain, Carthage can send a hundred black-winged warships sliding smoothly into the sea before the tide comes in!

We took apart the enemy's warship and understood the symbols the barbarians had carved on its planks. Roman hands can build the finest quinqueremes just as well, and with them we will seize the whole sea!

Assembling great ships from standard prefabricated parts is a marvel of classical engineering. By turning complex geometry into simple letters in a carpenter's hands, the shipbuilding workshops of Carthage led the world.
